headline: The Zimbabwean writer who won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing has denied using AI for his winning story, after a magazine reported that a detection tool rated it AI-made.
score_reason: Pool score kept: a prominent prize winner publicly answers an AI accusation and the prize is investigating, but the accusation rests on a detection tool whose accuracy is disputed.
importance_line: Writers, above all African writers who say they are scrutinised unfairly, and prize bodies are affected first, then publishers and makers of AI detectors, but the claim that the story is AI-written is unproven and disputed, and detectors can wrongly flag human writing.
summary: The BBC reports that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write his short story "The Blue Fighter", which won the £10,000 Caine Prize for African Writing a week ago, in reply to The Atlantic's report, which we carried on 12 Oct 2026, that the AI-detection tool Pangram rated the story as entirely AI-generated. Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, says the prize is investigating, with Kundizeza sending documentation about his drafts, and criticises The Atlantic for not waiting for a full investigation, while the Atlantic writer Vauhini Vara concedes that no detector, including Pangram, is 100% accurate.
notes: Full BBC text read. Reply story: Kundizeza answers The Atlantic's article by Vauhini Vara (published 11 Oct), which our 12 Oct 2026 edition carried as a headline-only item (item 95: 'The Atlantic reports that a short story that won the Caine Prize for African Writing seems to be the work of AI'). The claim is disputed and unproven.
